lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: practical: investigate how enzyme activity can be affected by changes in temperature

primer.text: Amylase digesting starch into maltose is the classic enzyme practical, and iodine is the clock: every droplet transfer that still turns blue-black means starch remains. This note runs the temperature version — water baths from 30 to 60 degrees, repeats for reliability, the reading of results, the two named limitations with fixes, and the CORMS planning frame.

modules.title: The amylase clock at different temperatures
modules.opening: The method is a timing race: starch solution is warmed to the chosen temperature, amylase joins it, and every minute a droplet is transferred to a well of iodine. Blue-black means starch survives; the first well that stays yellow-brown marks the moment digestion finished. Repeating at each temperature and across a range builds the dataset.
keyPoints: Amylase digests starch into maltose, and iodine tests for remaining starch.
Iodine is yellow-brown and turns blue-black only while starch is present.
A droplet is transferred to a fresh iodine well every minute until no colour change occurs.
The reaction time is read by counting the wells up to the first unchanged one.
The whole run is repeated across a temperature range such as 30 to 60 degrees Celsius.

low.restatement: Mix amylase with warmed starch; test droplets against iodine every minute; count wells until iodine stops turning blue-black — that count is the digestion time at that temperature.
low.analogy: Iodine wells are bus stops: the reaction's bus travels along them once per minute, and the first stop where nothing changes is its final stop.
low.examPointer: When describing the method, name the interval (every minute) and the readout (counting wells) — both carry marks.

medium.restatement: The design fixes volume and concentration while varying temperature, and the iodine-well count converts a continuous reaction into a discrete, comparable number; repeats at each temperature expose the random error the stopwatch cannot see.
medium.analogy: Counting wells turns a blur into a ruler: each well is one tick of ten seconds' worth of clock on the tile.
medium.examPointer: State the controlled variables (volumes, concentrations) explicitly when asked why the comparison is fair.

modules.title: Reading results, fixing limitations, planning with CORMS
modules.opening: The analysis reads the well counts as reaction speeds: fewer wells means faster digestion, with the shortest count at the optimum temperature. Two limitations matter — drifting water temperature and judging colour by eye — and each has a named fix. CORMS then wraps the whole design into a planning answer examiners can mark quickly.
keyPoints: The shortest iodine-well count marks the optimum temperature, where the enzyme works fastest.
Below the optimum, colder temperatures slow collisions and stretch the reaction time.
A named limitation is temperature drift, fixed by using proper water baths at each set temperature.
A second limitation is judging colour by eye, improved by a colorimeter that measures colour intensity.
CORMS stands for Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure and control variables.

low.restatement: Fewest wells = fastest = optimum. Fix drifting temperature with water baths; fix colour judgement with a colorimeter. CORMS plans the design.
low.analogy: The well count is a race time: the temperature that wins with the fewest ticks is the enzyme's favourite.
low.examPointer: Pair each limitation with its improvement — a limitation stated without a fix earns half the marks.

medium.restatement: The two limitations attack validity and precision respectively: drift confounds which temperature caused the rate, and subjective colour calls blur the endpoint; baths and a colorimeter target each directly.
medium.analogy: Drift is an unfair referee (the wrong team blamed), colour-judgement is a fuzzy scoreboard (nobody knows who won); baths fix the referee, the colorimeter sharpens the scoreboard.
medium.examPointer: In CORMS answers, give M its letter explicitly (M1 time via wells; M2 the count itself) — the note models that format.

glossary.definition: The multi-well plate holding separate iodine drops for each timed test.
An instrument that measures colour intensity by shining light through a solution.
The planning frame: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same/control variables.
